title: “You Feel It… But Is It Sin? The Question No One Dares to Answer Out Loud”
paragraphs:
“You Feel It… But Is It Sin? The Question No One Dares to Answer Out Loud”
When Desire Doesn’t Match Your Faith—And You’re Terrified to Ask God About It
There are thoughts you never say out loud.
Not in church. Not with your family. Not even in prayer.
Because the moment you admit it, even to yourself, it feels like something inside you might break.
What if… I’m attracted to the same sex?
And suddenly your entire identity feels like it’s standing in front of a courtroom—with no lawyer, no defense, just silence and fear.
You don’t choose the moment it starts. It just… happens.
A glance that lingers too long. A connection that feels deeper than it should. A quiet pull that doesn’t go away no matter how many worship songs you play or how many verses you try to memorize.
And then the question comes like a whisper you wish you could silence:
“Is this… sin?”
Not what you do. Not your actions.
But what you feel.
Because if even your feelings are sin… then where does that leave you?
And if they aren’t… then why does it feel so heavy?
Let’s not rush this.
Let’s sit in the tension for a moment.
Because Scripture doesn’t run from hard questions—and neither should we.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says something that shifts everything we thought we understood about sin:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν” (Matthew 5:28)
Translated carefully from the Greek, it means:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with the intent to desire her has already committed adultery in his heart.”
Notice what Jesus is doing.
He’s not condemning the existence of attraction.
He’s confronting the cultivation of desire.
There is a difference between a moment you experience… and a direction you choose.
The Greek word “ἐπιθυμῆσαι” (epithymēsai) is not passive—it’s intentional, nurtured longing.
So the question isn’t:
“Did you feel something?”
The deeper question is:
“What are you doing with what you felt?”
Because temptation itself is not sin.
Even Jesus was tempted.
Hebrews 4:15 says:
“πειρασθέντα κατὰ πάντα καθ᾽ ὁμοιότητα χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας”
“He was tempted in every way as we are—yet without sin.”
Temptation came.
It knocked.
But it never took residence.
That means attraction—whether toward the same sex or the opposite sex—is not, by itself, the final verdict of your soul.
It is a moment.
A signal.
A crossroad.
But not your identity.
Not your condemnation.
And definitely not beyond the reach of grace.
Now here’s where it gets real.
Because Scripture does not stay silent about sexual behavior.
Romans 1:26–27 speaks plainly about same-sex acts within the context of humanity turning away from God.
The Greek word used—“πάθη ἀτιμίας” (pathē atimias)—means “dishonorable passions,” pointing to desires that are acted upon in ways outside God’s design.
But don’t miss this.
The passage is not isolating one group of people as uniquely broken.
It is describing all humanity apart from God.
Because just a few verses later, Paul levels the ground:
“οὐκ ἔστιν δίκαιος, οὐδὲ εἷς” (Romans 3:10)
“There is no one righteous, not even one.”
So if you’re reading this thinking, “Does this mean I’m worse?”
No.
It means you’re human.
And humanity—every version of it—needs a Savior.
The enemy wants to trap you in one of two lies:
Either your attraction defines you completely…
Or your attraction disqualifies you completely.
But the Gospel destroys both.
Because in Christ, you are not your urges.
And you are not your shame.
You are someone being called.
Someone being pursued.
Someone being rewritten.
The Hebrew heart of Scripture echoes this truth in Psalm 51:10:
“לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים”
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Not “reward me for already being clean.”
Not “accept me as I am and leave me unchanged.”
But “create.”
Because transformation is not self-made.
It is God-breathed.
So is it sin to be attracted to the same sex?
No.
But like every human desire, it becomes spiritually dangerous when it is embraced, nurtured, and acted upon outside the will of God.
And here’s the part most people won’t tell you:
Following Jesus has never been about which desires you have.
It has always been about which desires you surrender.
Luke 9:23—straight from the Greek:
“ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν… καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι”
“Deny yourself… and follow Me.”
Not deny your existence.
Not deny your humanity.
But deny the version of yourself that tries to live without God’s authority.
And that applies to everyone.
Every craving.
Every longing.
Every hidden thought.
This is not a message of rejection.
It’s a call to something deeper.
Because Jesus never looked at someone trapped in sin and said, “Stay there.”
But He also never said, “You’re too far gone.”
He said, “Follow Me.”
And following Him means walking through tension.
It means nights where you wrestle.
Moments where you don’t understand yourself.
Days where obedience feels heavier than comfort.
But it also means something else.
Freedom.
Real freedom.
Not the kind that tells you to do whatever you feel.
But the kind that frees you from being controlled by what you feel.
Sit with it.
Let it speak.
And be honest…
When you read this, did something inside you quietly whisper, “That’s me”?
If it did, don’t hide.
You’re not the only one fighting.
And you were never meant to fight alone.
Someone who won’t judge but will walk with you.
Because supporting this mission isn’t about money.
It’s about multiplying truth.
It’s about making sure messages like this reach the next person before shame convinces them to give up.
Because this isn’t about labeling you.
It’s about leading you.
To the One who sees everything you’re afraid to admit…
And still chose the cross.
You are not the question you’re asking.
You are the person Jesus is still calling.
And He’s not finished with you yet.
Somewhere between your struggle and your surrender… grace is already rewriting your story.
